analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card rate hikes based on unrelated credit problems and requires clear minimum-payment cost disclosures.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, credit card companies could raise your interest rate because of a late payment on some other bill, a drop in your credit score, or other problems on your credit report — a practice known as 'universal default' — even if you always paid that card on time. This bill would have banned that, letting card issuers raise rates only because of what you did on that specific account. It also would have required every monthly statement to show, in a prominent table, how many months and how much total money it would take to pay off the balance if you only made the minimum payment.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of credit card holders, especially people carrying a balance who pay on time on that card but have imperfect credit elsewhere in their lives. They would keep their rate from being raised over events unrelated to the account, and the new statement disclosures would show them the true long-run cost of paying only the minimum, making it easier to see why minimum payments keep them in debt for years.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits creditors from using adverse information about a consumer — anything in a credit report or a change in the consumer's credit score — to raise a credit card's interest rate, unless the reason is directly related to that specific account [S2][S3].

Each monthly statement would have to show the minimum payment as a dollar amount and a percentage of the balance, how many months it would take to pay off the balance paying only the minimum, and the total cost of doing so [S2][S3].
Those disclosures would have to appear in a table, in at least 10-point type, in a prominent spot on the first page of the statement, so cardholders actually see them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers would give up a major way of raising rates — repricing accounts based on outside credit information — which was a significant revenue source. Issuers would also bear the cost of redesigning statements to carry the new disclosures.

drawbacks.text: Restricting rate increases to account-specific behavior could lead issuers to charge higher starting rates across the board, since they could no longer reprice risk after issuing the card — a cost borne by cardholders who never miss a payment anywhere [S2][S3].
Disclosure rules only inform; they do not lower anyone's payment. A cardholder seeing the decades-long cost of minimum payments on a statement still has to find a way to pay more each month.
Issuers and lenders would face compliance costs to rework billing statements and rate-setting systems, costs that could be passed on through fees or terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no rate hikes over problems on other accounts or general credit-score dips — directly addresses a practice that could turn an on-time cardholder's rate from single digits to 30% overnight. The honest counterargument is real: if issuers can't reprice risk later, they may price more risk up front, so the safest borrowers could see somewhat higher initial rates. On balance, the bill targeted a widely disliked practice and paired it with disclosures that make the cost of minimum payments visible; its main weakness is that disclosure alone doesn't reduce anyone's debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, passed along to its consumer credit subcommittee, and never moved from there before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey introduced the bill on August 3, 2007 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, which held no further action on it [S5].

On September 5, 2007, it was referred to the subcommittee handling financial institutions and consumer credit, where it remained with no markup, no floor vote, and no action of any kind through the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009 [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, who kept the ability to raise rates based on credit report information and credit score changes without any of the disclosure requirements taking effect.

for.name: Rep. Nita M. Lowey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban universal default and require minimum-payment cost disclosures on statements.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no markup, no vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 5, 2007 and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Democrat, was involved, and no cosponsors signed on and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: Universal default let issuers raise rates on customers based on outside credit information; the bill would have cut off that revenue channel and forced new statement disclosures. The industry's interest in keeping this practice ran directly against cardholders' pocketbooks.
